cover.instructions: Fill in the report cover. Title should be 'Stock Initiation Report'. Subtitle is the full company name. Eyebrow is a short context line (e.g., 'Stock Initiation · <date>'). Ticker is the stock ticker symbol. Tagline is a one-sentence neutral framing of the report — never an investment verdict, never first-person. tldr is a list of 1–3 short paragraphs capturing the punchline as a neutral observation of what the data shows; tldr_label can be left null to use the default 'TL;DR'. Key metrics (rendered in the doc-meta strip below the title): include current stock price (with recent % change), market cap, P/E ratio, and 1–2 other metrics most relevant to this company. The consensus rating, mean analyst target, and implied upside are SERVER-BUILT from deterministic facts — do not author them in prose.

sections.title: Company Overview
sections.instructions: Provide a concise profile of the company. Include: full company name, ticker symbol, year founded, headquarters location, main products or services, and number of employees. Present this as a brief narrative paragraph followed by a metric cards block with key company facts.

sections.title: Industry Overview
sections.instructions: Cover two areas. First, define what industry the company operates in and describe its current state: are there government incentives or restrictions? What factors are driving or constraining the industry? Second, quantify the market: what is the total addressable market size (in dollars)? What has the historical market CAGR been over the past 5 years? What is the projected future growth rate, and what factors drive that growth? What is the estimated market size by the target year? Use a combo chart or area chart to show historical and projected market size over time.

sections.title: Products and Services
sections.instructions: Cover two areas. First, for each major product or service line: what customer pain point does it address? How does the company's solution work? What differentiates it from alternatives? If the company has multiple product lines, describe each separately. Second, show the revenue breakdown. You MUST cite the deterministic facts `segment_revenue_latest` and `segment_share_latest` by name in your prose for the most recent fiscal year mix; do NOT reconstruct segment numbers from memory and do NOT staple a prior-year mix onto the headline FY label. Where `segment_revenue_yoy` is available, cite per-segment growth from it. Use a pie or donut chart showing each segment's share of the most recent fiscal year revenue, and a brief table with revenue figures and growth rates per segment. If the segment facts are null, OMIT the chart and table rather than fabricate.

sections.title: Business Model
sections.instructions: Explain how the company makes money. Identify all key stakeholders (suppliers, customers, partners, distributors) and describe the relationships between them. If the company sells physical products, describe the supply chain: who are the upstream suppliers, what does the company do, and who are the downstream buyers? Identify where the company sits in this chain. If the company provides services, explain the revenue model (subscription, transaction fees, licensing, advertising, etc.) and how money flows. You MUST cite the deterministic facts `segment_revenue_latest`, `segment_share_latest`, and `segment_revenue_yoy` by name when describing the revenue mix and where growth is concentrated; do NOT reconstruct the segment split from memory. Use `fiscal_year_end_latest` to label the period the mix corresponds to. Use text to explain, supported by metric cards for key business metrics (e.g., gross margin, customer count, ARPU, retention rate).

sections.title: Competitive Analysis
sections.instructions: Cover three areas. First, identify the main competitors and provide a brief profile of each (what they do, their key strengths). Second, create a comparison table across multiple dimensions: market share, revenue, growth rate, profitability, key product differentiators, geographic presence, and any other relevant factors. Use cell formatting to highlight where the target company leads or lags. Third, assess the company's moat (if any): does it have network effects, switching costs, cost advantages, intangible assets (brands, patents), or efficient scale? Be specific about what the moat is and how durable it appears.

sections.title: Management Team
sections.instructions: Cover two areas. First, profile the key executives (CEO, CFO, CTO, and other critical roles): their educational background, prior experience, tenure at the company, and notable achievements. Present this as a table with columns for name, title, background, and tenure. Second, flag any concerns: are there integrity issues, frequent executive turnover, related-party transactions, regulatory actions against management, or other governance red flags? If there are none, state that explicitly.

sections.title: Competitive Advantages and Weaknesses
sections.instructions: Provide a structured assessment of the company's strengths and weaknesses across these dimensions: product quality and differentiation, business model durability, sales and distribution channels, management team quality, technology and R&D capability, and financial position. Use a two-column group layout: one side listing advantages (strengths), the other listing disadvantages (weaknesses). Use text blocks with bullet points. End with a key finding block summarizing the net competitive position.

sections.title: Risk Analysis
sections.instructions: Analyze risks across three categories. Industry risks: potential adverse government policies, supply chain bottlenecks, emerging technologies or substitutes that could displace the company's products, and potential new competitors. Operational risks: management stability, integrity concerns, recent acquisitions and integration uncertainty, product mass-production challenges, and known or potential legal/litigation risks. Financial risks: balance sheet health and going-concern risk, auditor changes or CFO departures, trajectory of losses, cash runway (can the company sustain operations?), whether capital can support investment needs over the next 5 years, and ability to raise additional funding or debt. Present each category as a separate subsection with a text block. Use a rating badge or key finding block to summarize overall risk level (Low / Moderate / High / Very High).

sections.title: Recent Developments
sections.instructions: Cover the LAST 30 DAYS ONLY. Anything older than 30 days belongs in `historical_financials` discontinuities or does not belong in this report at all. Surface qualitative context that a reader would need to assess the stock today: company-specific news from the last 30 days (product launches, executive moves, M&A, guidance updates, material filings), recent analyst actions in the last 30 days (rating or PT changes with the analyst/firm named), regulatory or legal developments in the last 30 days, and sector or macro events that moved the thesis in the last 30 days. This section is qualitative and time-sensitive — structured tools do not cover it, so call `web_search` to gather sources. Cite each item inline with `[source, date, url]`. Drop any item whose source date is more than 30 days before the report date. If genuinely nothing material has happened in the last 30 days, state that explicitly with a 'no material developments in the last 30 days as of <date>' line rather than padding with older items.

sections.title: Historical Financial Data
sections.instructions: Cover four areas. First, state the company's fiscal year end date by citing `fiscal_year_end_latest` directly. Second, present a 5-year balance sheet summary table (total assets, total liabilities, shareholders' equity, cash and equivalents, total debt, and other material items). Third, present a 5-year income statement summary table (revenue, cost of revenue, gross profit, operating income, net income, EPS, revenue growth rate YoY, EPS growth rate YoY). Apply directional cell formatting to growth rates. When describing the mix that drives revenue, you MUST cite the deterministic facts `segment_revenue_latest` and `segment_share_latest` by name and the year referenced MUST match `fiscal_year_end_latest`; do NOT reconstruct segment figures from memory. Fourth, if there were any mergers, acquisitions, divestitures, or spin-offs during this period that caused significant changes in revenue or profit, explain them in a text block. Use combo charts to visualize revenue and margin trends over the 5-year period.

sections.title: Financial Analysis
sections.instructions: Cover three areas. First, present a table of income statement margin ratios over time (gross margin, operating margin, net margin, EBITDA margin) and visualize trends with a line chart. Second, evaluate financial health using: current ratio, quick ratio, debt-to-equity ratio, interest coverage ratio, operating cash flow to current liabilities ratio, and operating cash flow to net income ratio. State whether the company's finances are healthy and explain any concerns. Third, create a peer comparison table showing the target company vs. competitors on: accounts receivable turnover days, inventory turnover days, and accounts payable turnover days. Use cell formatting to highlight where the company stands relative to peers.

sections.title: Financial Projections
sections.instructions: Present a 3-year financial forecast including projected revenue, revenue growth rate, operating income, net income, and EPS for each year. Show assumptions behind the projections (e.g., segment growth drivers, margin expansion or compression, capital expenditure plans). Use a table for the forecast figures with directional formatting on growth rates, and a combo chart showing projected revenue bars with a margin trend line overlay. If consensus analyst estimates are available, compare the projections to consensus.

sections.title: Valuation Analysis
sections.instructions: Present THREE deterministic-helper-derived ranges side-by-side and let the reader compare. Do NOT synthesize them into a single OpenLIA price target. Do NOT pick a target multiple yourself. The three required blocks are: (1) Peer-multiple implied range — cite the helper fact `peer_multiple_implied_range` by name; render it as `metric_cards` or a `table` with low/median/high implied prices from peer P/E and EV/EBITDA percentiles. (2) Historical P/E band — cite the helper fact `historical_pe_band` (mean, +/-1 sigma, current percentile) by name; render it as a `chart:line` of the band over time with the current P/E marked. (3) Sourced sell-side range — cite the deterministic facts `analyst_target_high`, `analyst_target_mean`, `analyst_target_low`, and `analyst_count` by name; render as `metric_cards`. In addition, REQUIRED: emit a `football_field` exhibit overlaying the three ranges on a single horizontal-bar chart with the current price as a vertical reference line; cite the `football_field` helper fact by name. Prose presents the three ranges side-by-side (e.g., 'Peer-multiple implied range is $X–$Y; the historical P/E band suggests fair value of $Z; the sell-side range is $A–$B with mean $C [c1].') and DOES NOT synthesize them into a single OpenLIA target. Every numeric claim must come from a cited helper fact — do not perform multiplication, division, or growth calculations yourself.

sections.title: Analyst View
sections.instructions: Section name throughout the report is 'Analyst View'. The legacy internal id remains 'investment_recommendation' for backward compatibility with the runner / assembler / frontend section catalog; downstream renames are out of scope for this PR. Summarize the analyst landscape as INFORMATION GATHERED FROM SOURCES. Do NOT author your own rating or price target. The section MUST LEAD with these deterministic blocks in this order: (1) a `rating_badge` populated from `analyst_consensus_rating`, (2) a `metric_cards` block showing the consensus target band (mean / high / low / N analysts and implied upside) from `analyst_target_mean`, `analyst_target_high`, `analyst_target_low`, `analyst_count`, and `consensus_upside_pct`, (3) a `chart:bar` of `analyst_rating_distribution` (Strong Buy → Strong Sell counts). The server pre-builds these from EODHD AnalystRatings — leave them untouched. Add a fourth block: a `table` of recent rating changes in the last 90 days (Date, Firm, Action, From → To, Target Price), built from cited news entries surfaced by `web_search`/`get_company_news`. Every row MUST carry an inline `[N]` citation. If no rating-change events surfaced in the last 90 days, OMIT this table — never fabricate rows. Then a `comparison_split` with 'Bull-case arguments' (left) vs 'Bear-case arguments' (right). Every item MUST carry an inline `[N]` citation AND use sourced-voice verbs: 'JPMorgan rates', 'consensus reflects', 'management guided', 'the company disclosed', 'Bernstein argued', 'Goldman flagged', 'Barclays raised', 'Morgan Stanley initiated'. FORBIDDEN first-person voice (the P7 validator will reject the section): 'we believe', 'we view', 'we recommend', 'in our view', 'our base case', 'our rating', 'our target'. Close with a 3-4 sentence prose paragraph summarizing what the consensus reflects, citing sources. No first-person advocacy anywhere.

rail.instructions: Populate the Rail object. rail.verdict and rail.quick_stats are SERVER-BUILT from facts (analyst consensus rating and target come from EODHD AnalystRatings; quick_stats include Market Cap, Sector, Exchange, 52W Range, ADTV (3mo), and Forward P/E from the manifest). Do NOT author rail content directly. rail.sparkline (optional): 60-day daily close points labeled 'Last 60 days'.
